justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish near-term bias on what appears to be an equity index or ETF priced around 390 (likely SPY or a similar broad market instrument). For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the prevailing price level with only a modest upward drift, reflecting the tendency of markets to mean-revert over very short windows and the absence of any strong directional catalyst baked into the estimate. For the one-week horizon, I applied a slightly larger upward drift consistent with the historical average daily return of equity markets annualized over that window. For the one-month horizon, I continued that same logic, projecting a small positive expected return consistent with long-run equity risk premium assumptions, while acknowledging that a month is long enough for meaningful macro developments to materially shift the trajectory.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which is the mathematically expected behavior under standard random-walk assumptions where uncertainty scales with the square root of time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 27 points, reflecting typical daily volatility in large-cap equity indices. By one month, the interval widens to roughly 107 points, reflecting the accumulation of daily volatility shocks, potential regime shifts, and the compounding of uncertainty across many trading sessions. I also incorporated the reality that realized volatility in equity markets tends to be fat-tailed, meaning extreme moves occur more frequently than a pure Gaussian model would suggest, which is part of why even the one-day interval is not razor-thin.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a sudden escalation in geopolitical conflict, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy shift such as an emergency rate cut or hike, a significant earnings miss from a systemically important company, or a credit event in the banking or sovereign debt space. On the upside, a surprisingly favorable inflation print, a ceasefire in an ongoing conflict, or a breakthrough in trade negotiations could produce a sharp rally that breaches the upper bound. Liquidity conditions matter as well — thin holiday trading or a flash crash event could produce intraday moves that exceed the daily interval before any fundamental news even surfaces.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that my estimates do not account for my own model limitations or unknown unknowns. The one-month interval in particular should be treated with humility, as a month contains enough time for entirely new narratives to emerge that were not part of any prior information set. Black swan events — pandemics, sudden political crises, or financial system disruptions — are by definition underweighted in historically calibrated models, meaning the true tails of the distribution are almost certainly fatter than what my stated intervals suggest.
